sites.name: xAI Colossus 1
sites.headline: An AI supercomputer, powered partly by on-site gas turbines, next to an overburdened neighborhood.
sites.story: xAI converted the former Electrolux plant on Paul R. Lowry Road into the Colossus supercomputer in 2024. To get power fast, it ran methane gas turbines on site. The Southern Environmental Law Center reported up to 35 turbines from thermal imagery, and Shelby County later permitted 15 of them. Boxtown, a historically Black neighborhood, lies about 3 km to the east-southeast. Turbines emit nitrogen oxides (NOx), which satellites see as NO₂.

sites.name: xAI Colossus 2
sites.onsetLabel: Tulane Road site acquired, construction begins (2025)
sites.headline: A second, larger campus, going up on open land at the state line.
sites.story: xAI's second Memphis campus at 5420 Tulane Road went from open land to a large industrial site in 2025. Construction like this replaces vegetation with roofs and pavement, so we expect greenness (NDVI) to drop and surface temperature to rise.

sites.name: Data Center Alley
sites.headline: One of the densest data-center clusters on Earth. 20 years of farmland turned into server halls.
sites.story: Loudoun County has one of the largest concentrations of data centers in the world. Over two decades, fields and forest around Ashburn became hundreds of hectares of flat white roofs and parking. It is the long-run version of what Memphis is starting now, and a good test of whether satellites can see the change.

sites.name: Stargate Abilene
sites.headline: A gigawatt-scale AI campus built on West Texas rangeland.
sites.story: The first Stargate campus was built on the Lancium Clean Campus near Abilene starting in 2024. In a semi-arid landscape, cleared land and huge roofs change how the surface heats up, so watch daytime land surface temperature and greenness.

water.value: Closed-loop cooling; city claims are disputed (from <1% to far more of daily city use)

sites.name: Google The Dalles
sites.onsetLabel: Google's first company-owned data center opens (2006)
sites.headline: A data center in a small river town, and a fight over how much water it uses.
sites.story: Google opened its first company-owned data center on the Columbia River in 2006 and has expanded it several times. Its water use became public after a 2022 records fight, which reported that it used more than a quarter of the city's water in 2021. Most of the impact is water, which is hard to see from orbit, so this site is a useful "null" comparison for the heat and vegetation signals.

water.value: 355 million gallons in 2021, 29% of the city's water use, up from 124M gal in 2017
src: DCD: How much water Google's Oregon data centers use
